D017-D004_h005.question_both:
I’ve been struggling for about a year now, maybe longer, with this growing sense that something’s just… off about how I look. It started with my hair—I kept noticing it looked thin, patchy, like people could tell something was wrong even though no one says anything. Then it shifted to my teeth; I avoid smiling, even during sessions with clients. It’s hard, you know? As a social worker, I’m supposed to be present, but I catch myself checking reflections in windows or avoiding eye contact.

I’ve asked my colleagues a few times—casually, like, “Do I look normal today?” or “Does my hair seem weird?” Just to make sure I’m not imagining things. A couple of them said I look fine, but it doesn’t really sink in. I keep wondering if they’re just being kind. I don’t do anything extreme—no mirror-checking for hours or changing clothes constantly—but I do think about it a lot, especially before meetings. I can’t tell if it’s me being overly sensitive or if there’s actually something visible that everyone’s too polite to mention.
D017-D004_h005.question_a:
I’ve been a social worker for over twenty years, and lately, I’ve found it harder and harder to meet with clients because of how I look. My hair feels like it’s falling out unevenly, even though my doctor says it’s not—but I *know* there are thin patches near the crown, and it makes me look unprofessional, like I’m not in control. I check it constantly in mirrors, windows, even the reflection of my phone screen. I ask my colleagues all the time: “Does my hair look normal? Does it look like I’m losing it?” Most of them just say “fine” now, but I can tell they’re humoring me.

I spend at least an hour every morning styling it just right, parting it the same way, trying to cover what I know is there. If I miss a spot, I get incredibly anxious and have to redo it. I’ve canceled home visits because I couldn’t get it “just so.” I know I sound obsessive—maybe even irrational—but I *feel* it. The flaw is real to me, even if others don’t see it. The rituals calm the panic, but only for a little while.
D017-D004_h005.question_b:
I’ve been feeling really troubled for about the past year, maybe longer, about how I look—specifically my teeth and hair. I’m convinced they’re horribly misshapen, like something’s deeply wrong that people won’t say out loud. I know it sounds odd, but I can *feel* something’s off, even though my dentist says there’s nothing wrong, and my hairdresser keeps telling me it looks fine. Still, I don’t trust it. I ask my coworkers and friends all the time—“Does this look normal?”—I probably annoy them. I used to check in mirrors constantly, but honestly, I quit doing that because it didn’t help. I just *know* it’s bad. I still avoid certain angles in photos, though. 

It’s frustrating, but otherwise, I’m working full time as a social worker and handling my cases just fine. I even run a support group. The only real issue is how much this thought sticks with me—it won’t let go, no matter what anyone says. I know people think I’m being self-conscious, but to me, it’s not vanity. It’s reality.

For the past two years, I can’t stop thinking about how my nose looks—it feels huge, distorted, like it’s lopsided. I know people tell me it looks fine, that I’m imagining it, but I see it every time I pass a mirror or catch my reflection in a window. I take photos, but then I end up zooming in, convinced there’s swelling or a bump I need to fix. 

I spend hours a day checking, adjusting the lighting, comparing old pictures. Sometimes I pick at the skin around my nose, trying to smooth it out, even though it bleeds sometimes. I use makeup to cover redness, but I end up rubbing it raw. I haven’t gone out in weeks because I can’t stand the idea of someone seeing me like this. I know it sounds extreme, but I *feel* it—that flaw is real to me. And if I don’t do these things, I get so anxious I can’t focus on work, can’t function. It’s not just a thought—it’s something I have to act on.

I’ve looked in every mirror, taken countless selfies at different angles, zoomed in just to prove it’s there. My editor keeps asking why I keep missing deadlines, but how can I focus when I know it’s getting worse?

I don’t pick at my skin like I used to—stopped squeezing or trying to “fix” it with tweezers about six months ago. That didn’t help, and honestly, I realized the problem isn’t the skin. It’s the structure. I’ve read medical forums, even messaged a few plastic surgeons, but they don’t get it either. They talk about “perception issues,” but they’re not seeing what I see.

I still write, I pay my bills—life runs. But everything feels secondary to this truth I’m carrying. I just wish someone would acknowledge what’s clearly wrong with my face.
